content.title: What is Contract Testing?
content.explanation:
Contract testing ensures that an API provider and its consumers agree on the shape of their interactions. Unlike end-to-end tests that test the entire stack, contract tests verify that each consumer can trust the provider to deliver what it expects.

**The Testing Pyramid with Contracts:**

```
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │   End-to-End    │  Slow, brittle, expensive
                    │    (10% of tests)│  Critical user journeys only
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                    ┌────────▼────────┐
                    │   Contract      │  Fast, focused, consumer-driven
                    │   (30% of tests)│  Provider must satisfy all consumers
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                    ┌────────▼────────┐
                    │   Integration   │  API-level tests
                    │   (20% of tests)│  Provider-side verification
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                    ┌────────▼────────┐
                    │     Unit        │  Fastest, most numerous
                    │   (40% of tests)│  Isolated component tests
                    └─────────────────┘
```

**Why Contract Testing?**

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Provider changes break consumers | Contracts catch breaking changes before deployment |
| E2E tests are slow and flaky | Contract tests run in milliseconds |
| Which consumers use which fields? | Contracts document actual usage |
| API versioning complexity | Contracts enable safe evolution |
| Microservices coordination | Teams can work independently |

**Consumer-Driven Contracts (CDC):**

```
┌────────────┐     ┌────────────┐     ┌────────────┐
│ Consumer A │────▶│  Contract  │────▶│            │
└────────────┘     │   (Pact)   │     │  Provider  │
┌────────────┐     │            │     │            │
│ Consumer B │────▶│  { json }  │────▶│   Service  │
└────────────┘     └────────────┘     └────────────┘
       │                  │                  │
       │                  ▼                  │
       │           ┌────────────┐            │
       └──────────▶│ Continuous │◄───────────┘
                   │ Integration│
                   │   Pipeline │
                   └────────────┘
```

**Key Insight:** Contracts are living documentation that evolve with your consumers. They give you confidence to deploy the provider knowing you won't break existing consumers.

The Pact Broker is a central repository for sharing contracts and verification results. It enables teams to work independently while maintaining compatibility.

**Pact Broker Architecture:**

```
┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
│   Consumer   │────▶│     Pact     │◀────│   Provider   │
│   Pipeline   │     │    Broker    │     │   Pipeline   │
└──────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘
        │                   │                     │
        ▼                   ▼                     ▼
┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
│  Publish     │     │  Store &     │     │  Verify &    │
│  Contracts   │     │  Version     │     │  Publish     │
└──────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘
```

**Consumer CI/CD - Publish Contracts:**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/consumer-tests.yml
name: Consumer Tests
on: [push]

jobs:
  test-and-publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm test # Generates pact files
      
      - name: Publish to Pact Broker
        run: |
          npx pact-broker publish ./pacts \
            --consumer-app-version ${{ github.sha }} \
            --branch ${{ github.ref_name }} \
            --broker-base-url ${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_URL }} \
            --broker-token ${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN }}
      
      - name: Check if can be deployed
        run: |
          npx pact-broker can-i-deploy \
            --pacticipant WebFrontend \
            --version ${{ github.sha }} \
            --to-environment production \
            --broker-base-url ${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_URL }} \
            --broker-token ${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN }}
```

**Provider CI/CD - Verify Contracts:**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/provider-verification.yml
name: Provider Verification
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 * * * *' # Hourly verification

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:14
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm start & # Start provider
      
      - name: Run verification
        run: |
          npx pact-provider-verifier \
            --provider-base-url http://localhost:3000 \
            --pact-broker-base-url ${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_URL }} \
            --pact-broker-token ${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN }} \
            --provider-version ${{ github.sha }} \
            --provider-version-branch main \
            --publish-verification-results
      
      - name: Tag if verified
        if: success()
        run: |
          npx pact-broker create-version-tag \
            --pacticipant UserService \
            --version ${{ github.sha }} \
            --tag verified \
            --broker-base-url ${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_URL }} \
            --broker-token ${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN }}
```

**Deployment Safety with can-i-deploy:**

```bash
# Before deploying consumer to production
pact-broker can-i-deploy \
  --pacticipant WebFrontend \
  --version 1.2.3 \
  --to-environment production

# Before deploying provider to production
pact-broker can-i-deploy \
  --pacticipant UserService \
  --version 2.0.0 \
  --to-environment production

# Matrix check with multiple consumers
pact-broker can-i-deploy \
  --pacticipant UserService:version=2.0.0 \
  --pacticipant WebFrontend:version=1.2.3 \
  --pacticipant MobileApp:version=3.0.1 \
  --to-environment production
```

**Pact Broker Webhooks for CI:**

```javascript
// Configure webhook to trigger provider tests when consumer publishes
const webhook = {
  description: 'Trigger provider verification on consumer publish',
  events: [{ name: 'contract_content_changed' }],
  request: {
    method: 'POST',
    url: 'https://api.github.com/repos/your-org/provider-service/dispatches',
    headers: {
      'Authorization': 'token ${GITHUB_TOKEN}',
      'Accept': 'application/vnd.github.v3+json'
    },
    body: {
      event_type: 'pact_verification_required',
      client_payload: {
        consumer: '${pactbroker.consumerName}',
        version: '${pactbroker.consumerVersionNumber}'
      }
    }
  }
};
```

**Version Tags and Branches:**

| Tag | Purpose |
|-----|---------|
| `main` | Latest main branch build |
| `prod` | Currently in production |
| `verified` | Passed provider verification |
| `feature/xyz` | Feature branch |

**Key Insight:** The Pact Broker creates a feedback loop between consumers and providers. `can-i-deploy` prevents breaking changes from reaching production.

| Real-time streams | ✅ Yes, message pacts | Schema registry |

```
Phase 1: Foundation (Week 1-2)
├── Set up Pact Broker
├── Add first consumer test
└── Add provider verification

Phase 2: Critical Paths (Week 3-4)
├── Identify core service dependencies
├── Add contracts for critical flows
└── Integrate with CI/CD

Phase 3: Expansion (Week 5-8)
├── Add all consumer-service pairs
├── Implement can-i-deploy gates
└── Train teams on contract testing

Phase 4: Maturity (Week 9+)
├── Automate contract generation
├── Implement OpenAPI validation
├── Add performance baselines
└── Regular contract reviews
```

**Sample Contract Testing Policy:**

```markdown
# Contract Testing Policy

## Mandatory
- Every service that consumes another API must have Pact tests
- Every provider must verify all consumer contracts before deployment
- All contracts must be published to the Pact Broker
- `can-i-deploy` must pass before production deployment

## Best Practices
- Use matchers for all dynamic data
- Define provider states for each interaction
- Keep interactions focused (one logical test per interaction)
- Tag versions with branch names and environment
- Review contracts when making breaking changes

## Exceptions
- Public APIs use OpenAPI validation instead
- Third-party APIs use consumer-only contracts
- Real-time systems use message pacts
```

| Metric | Target | How to Measure |
|--------|--------|----------------|
| Contract coverage | >80% of service pairs | Pact Broker API |
| Verification time | <5 minutes | CI pipeline time |
| Breaking changes caught | 100% | can-i-deploy failures |
| Deployment confidence | High | Team surveys |
| E2E test reduction | 50% | Test count comparison |

# Publish contracts
pact-broker publish ./pacts \
  --consumer-app-version $VERSION \
  --branch $BRANCH \
  --broker-base-url $URL \

content.title: What is Fuzz Testing?
content.explanation:
Fuzz testing (fuzzing) is an automated testing technique that involves providing invalid, unexpected, or random data as inputs to an API. The goal is to find crashes, memory leaks, assertion failures, and unexpected behaviors that could lead to security vulnerabilities or stability issues.

**Types of Fuzzing:**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      FUZZING TYPES                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  Generation Fuzzing:                                             │
│  └── Creates inputs from scratch based on specifications         │
│                                                                   │
│  Mutation Fuzzing:                                               │
│  └── Modifies valid inputs to create variations                  │
│                                                                   │
│  Protocol Fuzzing:                                               │
│  └── Tests protocol-level conformance and edge cases             │
│                                                                   │
│  Smart Fuzzing:                                                  │
│  └── Uses heuristics and feedback to guide input generation      │
│                                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Why Fuzz APIs?**

| Reason | Example | Impact |
|--------|---------|--------|
| **Find edge cases** | 64-bit integers, Unicode, emoji | Crashes, data corruption |
| **Security vulnerabilities** | Buffer overflows, injection | Remote code execution |
| **Denial of service** | Deeply nested JSON, large payloads | Resource exhaustion |
| **Business logic flaws** | Negative quantities, future dates | Financial loss |

**The Fuzzing Loop:**

```
┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│  Generate   │───▶│  Send to    │───▶│  Monitor    │
│   Input     │    │    API      │    │  Response   │
└─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘
        ▲                                    │
        │                                    │
        └────────────────────────────────────┘
              Analyze and mutate
```

**Key Insight:** Fuzzing finds the bugs you didn't know to look for. It's not about testing expected behavior—it's about breaking things intentionally.

Penetration testing is a simulated attack against your API to identify vulnerabilities that an attacker could exploit. Unlike automated scanning, penetration testing involves manual techniques and creative thinking.

**The Penetration Testing Phases:**

```

│                    PEN TEST METHODOLOGY                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  1. RECONNAISSANCE                                               │

│         • API documentation, endpoints, authentication           │
│         • Technology stack, version information                  │

content.title: What is API Reliability?
content.explanation:
API reliability is the probability that your API will perform its intended function without failure over a specified period. It's about consistency, availability, and resilience.

**Key Reliability Metrics:**

| Metric | Definition | Target |
|--------|------------|--------|
| **Availability** | Percentage of time API is operational | 99.9% (8.76h downtime/year) |
| **Uptime** | Time between failures | 99.99% (52m downtime/year) |
| **MTBF** | Mean time between failures | > 30 days |
| **MTTR** | Mean time to recover | < 1 hour |
| **SLA** | Service Level Agreement | Contractual guarantee |
| **SLO** | Service Level Objective | Internal target |
| **SLI** | Service Level Indicator | Measured metric |

**Reliability Testing Pyramid:**

```
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │   Production    │  Canary deployments
                    │   Verification  │  Real traffic monitoring
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                    ┌────────▼────────┐
                    │   Load Testing  │  Performance under stress
                    │   (20% of tests)│  Scalability validation
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                    ┌────────▼────────┐
                    │  Chaos Testing  │  Failure injection
                    │  (15% of tests) │  Resilience validation
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                    ┌────────▼────────┐

                    │  Unit Tests     │  Circuit breaker tests
                    │  (50% of tests) │  SLA validation
                    └─────────────────┘
```

**Key Insight:** Reliability isn't just about being up—it's about being consistently available and performing correctly under all conditions.

content.title: What is Data Integrity?
content.explanation:
Data integrity ensures that data remains accurate, consistent, and reliable throughout its lifecycle. For APIs, this means that create, read, update, and delete operations maintain data correctness.

**The ACID Properties:**

| Property | Description | API Example |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| **Atomicity** | All or nothing | Create order + update inventory both succeed or fail |
| **Consistency** | Data follows rules | Email format valid, foreign keys exist |
| **Isolation** | Concurrent operations don't interfere | Two users updating same record |
| **Durability** | Committed data persists | Data survives crashes |

**Consistency Models:**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    CONSISTENCY MODELS                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  Strong Consistency:                                             │
│  └── All reads see the most recent write                         │
│      • ACID databases                                             │
│      • Bank transactions                                          │
│                                                                   │
│  Eventual Consistency:                                           │
│  └── Reads may see stale data, but will converge                 │
│      • DNS                                                        │
│      • Distributed databases (Cassandra)                         │
│                                                                   │
│  Read-Your-Writes:                                               │
│  └── A user sees their own writes immediately                    │
│      • Session consistency                                        │
│                                                                   │
│  Monotonic Reads:                                                │
│  └── Reads don't go back in time                                 │
│      • Versioned data                                             │
│                                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Key Insight:** Different APIs need different consistency guarantees. Choose the right model and test that it's actually implemented.
